name: Dermaplaning razor

lead: Dermaplaning is mechanical exfoliation with a single sharp blade drawn lightly across the face to remove dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, or peach fuzz. People do it for an instantly smoother, brighter surface and makeup that sits more evenly.

The blade shaves the outer layer of skin and the fine hair at skin level, and exfoliation lets skincare products absorb more easily. The hair follicle is untouched, so hair regrows on its normal schedule. A 2011 systematic review described the data on dermaplaning as scarce and largely anecdotal, and lab studies show it removes part of the stratum corneum.

paras: Home users pull a small facial razor at a shallow angle over dry, clean skin, usually every few weeks, before skincare or makeup. Professionals use a sterile scalpel-style blade. Results last on the order of weeks as skin and hair regrow, and the razors cost about $10 to $20.
Risks include nicks, irritation and breakouts, and it is not advised over active acne or inflamed skin. Hair does not grow back thicker or darker. A clean blade reduces infection risk.

chain: Blade removes dead cells and peach fuzz
angle.text: A single blade removes peach fuzz and dead skin in one pass, so skin looks smoother and brighter and makeup applies more evenly right away. The effect lasts a few weeks as skin and hair regrow.

lead: Dermaplaning is a form of mechanical exfoliation in which a single sharp blade is drawn at a shallow angle across the face to remove the outermost layer of dead skin cells and fine vellus hair, commonly called peach fuzz. Clinicians and aestheticians perform it with a sterile surgical-style blade, and consumer versions are small single-blade facial razors sold for home use, typically at around $10 to $20 [1][2].

People use it to get a smoother, brighter-looking skin surface and a more even base for makeup and skincare products: the blade removes surface scale and hair, so light reflects more evenly and products sit more smoothly [1][2]. Reported effects last on the order of weeks, since the skin and hair regrow [1][3].

Published research is limited. A 2011 systematic review of dermaplaning, topical oxygen and light therapy found that the data supporting these noninvasive facial rejuvenation methods were scarce and largely anecdotal [4]. Laboratory studies show that dermaplaning removes part of the stratum corneum and can alter how drugs permeate excised skin [5][6], and older surgical literature describes dermatome-based dermaplaning for acne scarring [7][8]. No controlled trial of the home facial razor for cosmetic smoothing is known.
infobox: Sterile scalpel-type blade used by clinicians and aestheticians [3]
A few minutes to about 1.5 hours depending on area [3]

paras: Home dermaplaning razors are small blades with a protective guard or handle designed for use on the face, while professional dermaplaning is performed by dermatologists, plastic surgeons or licensed aestheticians with a sterile blade [1][3]. Accounts of the technique describe holding the skin taut and drawing the blade in light strokes at a shallow angle, usually around 45 degrees [1]. It is generally described as a cosmetic exfoliation, distinct from chemical peels and microdermabrasion because it uses a manual blade and removes vellus hair at the same time [1][2].

Cleveland Clinic describes dermaplaning as a minimally invasive procedure in which a provider shaves off the uppermost layers of skin, used mainly for acne scars and dull skin, with some people using it for hair removal. Numbing cream or spray may be used beforehand, the procedure is usually not painful, and a soothing gel or ointment may be applied afterward [3]. Home razors apply the same principle at the very superficial level without a clinician.

The blade scrapes away the stratum corneum, the dead outer layer of skin, together with fine hair cut at the skin surface [1]. Histological work on dermaplaned skin has shown removal of the stratum corneum and parts of the viable epidermis [5]. Because the blade cuts hair at the surface, descriptions of the technique state that follicles are not altered and vellus hair regrows in its original fine form after a few weeks [1]. Wikipedia's exfoliation article notes that dermaplaning specialists reject the belief that shaving makes hair grow back thicker, and that dermaplaning does not stimulate collagen [2].

A laboratory study found that four strokes of a dermaplaning device caused a significant drop in the skin's electrical resistance, indicating loss of barrier function of the stratum corneum, and increased 24-hour permeation of two model drugs through excised skin, although absorption varied between samples [5]. A separate in vitro study compared dermaplaning with sonophoresis, laser, microneedles and microdermabrasion as ways to enhance transdermal delivery of naloxone, finding that all of these techniques shortened lag time compared with untreated skin [6]. These studies concern drug delivery models and not cosmetic outcomes.

Dermaplaning appears in the medical literature from at least the 1970s. Papers from 1977 describe dermaplaning, including with an electrokeratome device, as part of operations to level and revise the acne-scarred face, often combined with excision or chemical peeling [7][8]. A 1977 plastic surgery paper noted that treatments for acne pitting were often disappointing and advised surgeons to promise patients little improvement [8]. Another 1977 paper describes dermatome dermaplaning together with excision for sycosis nuchae, a scarring condition of the neck [9]. A 1980 review listed dermaplaning among alternatives to excisional surgery for facial skin lesions [10].

A 2013 case report lists dermaplaning among the techniques used for rhinophyma, alongside newer tools [11]. One AI-generated encyclopedia summary says the technique entered mainstream skincare in the 2010s through social media and celebrity endorsement, with the hashtag reportedly reaching billions of views by 2024 [1]; this comes from an untrusted secondary source and was not independently verified.

Wikipedia covers dermaplaning within its article on cosmetic exfoliation, where it is listed as a mechanical method that uses a single-blade tool to remove dead skin and fine facial hair, alongside scrubs, brushes, waxing and wet shaving, and distinct from chemical peels, ablative laser resurfacing and dermabrasion [2]. The article says it is marketed as improving texture and helping skin absorb products better, and that aestheticians are the recommended providers [2].

Practitioners of exfoliation describe it as promoting a deeper cleanse and younger-looking skin; dermatologists quoted in the same article say exfoliation is not medically necessary because dead skin sheds naturally, and that over-exfoliating can weaken the skin barrier, raise infection risk and cause tightness, sensitivity or redness [2]. These are general statements about exfoliation, not dermaplaning-specific trial results.

sections.h: How people use it for their looks
paras: The appearance chain people describe is: the blade lifts dead surface cells and peach fuzz, light reflects more evenly from the smoother surface, and foundation and skincare sit more smoothly on the face [1][2]. Home users apply it every few weeks as the vellus hair regrows, and professionals offer it as a stand-alone facial or as a preparation step before peels or other treatments, according to descriptions of the technique [1].

Cleveland Clinic says it can soften the look of acne scars, fine lines and dull skin, revealing smoother, firmer skin, but that it does not stop aging and any hair removal is temporary [3]. Some people have multiple sessions to reach their goals, with skin allowed to heal fully between treatments [3].

The 2011 systematic review identified 42 peer-reviewed English-language manuscripts on dermaplaning, oxygen therapy and light therapy, and concluded that the scientific data supporting them were scarce, anecdotal and not well documented, even though the treatments had grown popular with patients and practitioners [4]. Reported benefits such as a smoother surface, immediate brightness and easier makeup application rest mainly on practitioner and aesthetics-industry accounts [1]. The immediate removal of hair and surface scale is a direct physical effect of the blade; its duration and any longer-term skin-quality effects have not been measured in published trials.
A 2011 systematic review in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery screened dermaplaning, topical oxygen and photodynamic therapy literature and found the evidence scarce and anecdotal [4].

Historical surgical papers from 1977 describe dermaplaning as one step in managing acne scarring and sycosis nuchae, using dermatomes rather than consumer razors [7][8][9]. A 2013 case report mentions dermaplaning and dermabrasion among techniques for rhinophyma [11].
No randomized controlled trial of home facial dermaplaning razors for skin appearance has been found.

Cleveland Clinic describes dermaplaning as generally safe and lists infection, scarring (keloid or hypertrophic) and skin discoloration as risks; it says people with active acne, cold sores, eczema, psoriasis, contact dermatitis, moles, skin tags or radiation burns should discuss it with a provider first [3]. Descriptions of the procedure also say it is not generally advised soon after isotretinoin use [1]. Reported risks include nicks and cuts, temporary redness, irritation and breakouts, and increased sun sensitivity afterwards, with sunscreen commonly recommended by practitioners [1][3]. Using unclean blades is associated with infection risk [1].

After the professional procedure, Cleveland Clinic describes redness and swelling settling over the first week, possible tightness and pinkness in the second, and sun avoidance for weeks to months until skin returns to its normal color [3]. Some sources report that dermaplaning does not cause hair to grow back thicker or darker [1][2]; Cleveland Clinic lists hair regrowth as something to ask a provider about [3].

Dermaplaning appears on looksmax.org in a how-to guide that presents it as a low-cost skincare step for a smoother-looking face and for helping products absorb, paired with a cleanser, toner and moisturizer [12]. It is discussed as a low-cost step for smoother-looking skin and makeup application, alongside other exfoliation and skincare methods.

Home dermaplaning razors are typically sold in multi-packs with replaceable blades at about $10 to $20. Features that vary include blade guard design, handle length and whether blades are single-use or replaceable.
